Bonding.intro: Atoms bond together to form compounds. There are three main types of chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic.

sections.title: Types of Bond
points: Ionic bonding — transfer of electrons between metal and non-metal; forms ions
Covalent bonding — sharing of electrons between non-metals
Metallic bonding — sea of delocalised electrons between positive metal ions

callout.label: Why Bond?
callout.text: Atoms bond to achieve a full outer electron shell (usually 8 — octet rule). Bonding makes atoms more stable.

keyTerms.def: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
Electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons

examTips: Ionic = metal + non-metal. Covalent = non-metal + non-metal. Metallic = metal + metal.
Always draw dot-and-cross diagrams showing full outer shells for ionic and covalent bonding.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that in ionic bonding, electrons are TRANSFERRED (not shared).

Ionic Compounds.intro: Ionic compounds form when electrons are transferred from metals to non-metals, creating oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic forces.

sections.title: Forming Ions
points: Metal loses electrons → forms positive ion (cation)
Non-metal gains electrons → forms negative ion (anion)
Ions have full outer electron shells — stable configuration
Examples: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻, O²⁻

sections.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
points: High melting/boiling points — strong electrostatic forces need a lot of energy to overcome
Conduct electricity when dissolved in water or molten — ions free to move
Do NOT conduct when solid — ions held in fixed positions
Often soluble in water — water molecules can surround and separate the ions

keyTerms.def: An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and has a charge
A positively charged ion formed when a metal loses electrons
A negatively charged ion formed when a non-metal gains electrons
Regular arrangement of ions in an ionic compound

examTips: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when MOLTEN or in SOLUTION — not when solid.
Higher charge on ions = stronger force = higher melting point (e.g. MgO higher than NaCl).
commonMistakes: Saying ionic compounds conduct electricity as solids — they don't, ions can't move.
Forgetting that ALL ionic compounds have high melting points.

Covalent Substances.intro: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share electrons. Covalent substances can have simple molecular or giant covalent structures.

sections.title: Simple Molecular Substances
points: Small molecules held together by STRONG covalent bonds
Molecules held to each other by WEAK intermolecular forces
Low melting/boiling points — weak forces easy to overcome
Do NOT conduct electricity — no charged particles
Examples: H₂O, CO₂, O₂, NH₃, CH₄

sections.title: Giant Covalent Structures
points: Millions of atoms covalently bonded in a 3D lattice
Very high melting/boiling points — many strong covalent bonds to break
Do NOT conduct electricity (except graphite)
Examples: diamond (hardest natural substance), silicon dioxide (sand), graphite, graphene

sections.title: Diamond vs Graphite
points: Diamond — each C bonded to 4 others; tetrahedral; very hard; no free electrons; doesn't conduct
Graphite — each C bonded to 3 others in layers; 1 delocalised electron per atom; conducts electricity; layers slide (lubricant)

keyTerms.def: Substance made of small covalently bonded molecules with weak forces between them
Substance with millions of atoms bonded covalently in a lattice
An electron not associated with a specific atom — can move freely
A force between molecules — weaker than the bonds within molecules

examTips: Simple molecular = low MP. Giant covalent = very high MP.
Graphite conducts because it has delocalised electrons — diamond does not conduct.
When explaining properties, distinguish between bonds WITHIN molecules and forces BETWEEN molecules.
commonMistakes: Saying covalent substances have high melting points — simple molecular ones do NOT (giant covalent ones do).
Forgetting graphite is the exception — it DOES conduct electricity.

Metallic Structures.intro: Metals have a unique bonding structure that explains their characteristic properties.

sections.title: Metallic Bonding
points: Positive metal ions in a regular lattice
Surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons
Strong electrostatic attraction between ions and electrons
Explains properties: conduction, malleability, high melting point

sections.title: Properties of Metals
points: High melting/boiling points — strong metallic bonds
Good conductors of electricity — delocalised electrons carry charge
Good conductors of heat — delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy
Malleable and ductile — layers of ions can slide without breaking bonds (electrons move too)
Alloys — different-sized atoms disrupt regular arrangement, making it harder to slide → stronger

keyTerms.def: Attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
A mixture of a metal with another element to improve properties
Ability to be hammered into shape without breaking

examTips: Always link metallic properties back to delocalised electrons for conduction, and ion layers sliding for malleability.
Alloys are harder than pure metals because different-sized atoms disrupt the regular structure.
commonMistakes: Saying metals conduct because they have free electrons — say 'delocalised electrons'.
Forgetting that alloys are harder because of disrupted layers.

Polymers.intro: Polymers are large molecules made of many repeating units (monomers) joined together. They have distinctive properties.

sections.title: Polymer Structure
points: Monomer = small repeating unit
Polymer = long chain of monomers joined by covalent bonds
Examples: poly(ethene) from ethene; nylon; PVC; DNA; proteins
Thermosoftening polymers — chains with weak intermolecular forces; melt when heated; remoulded
Thermosetting polymers — cross-links between chains; don't melt; rigid

keyTerms.def: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units
A small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer
Polymer that softens/melts when heated; can be reshaped
Polymer with cross-links; does not melt; stays rigid when heated

examTips: Thermosoftening = no cross-links = melts. Thermosetting = cross-links = doesn't melt.
Useful property of thermosetting plastics: can withstand high temperatures (e.g. electrical fittings, pan handles).
commonMistakes: Confusing the two types of polymer — remember cross-links = thermosetting = rigid.

States of Matter.intro: The three states of matter — solid, liquid and gas — have different particle arrangements and properties. Changes of state involve energy changes.

sections.title: Particle Model
points: Solid — particles close together, regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions
Liquid — particles close together, random arrangement, move freely but stay together
Gas — particles far apart, random arrangement, move fast in all directions

sections.title: Changes of State
points: Melting: solid → liquid (energy absorbed)
Boiling/evaporation: liquid → gas (energy absorbed)
Condensing: gas → liquid (energy released)
Freezing: liquid → solid (energy released)
Changes of state = PHYSICAL changes — no new substance formed

keyTerms.def: Temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid
Temperature at which a substance changes from liquid to gas throughout
A change of state — reversible, no new substance formed

examTips: Changes of state are PHYSICAL not chemical — no new substance formed, easily reversible.
At melting/boiling point, temperature stays constant — energy goes into breaking forces between particles.
commonMistakes: Saying changes of state are chemical changes — they are physical.
Forgetting that at melting/boiling point temperature stays CONSTANT.

Nanoparticles.intro: Nanoparticles are extremely small particles, 1-100 nanometres in size. Their tiny size gives them unique properties compared to the same material in bulk.

sections.title: Properties of Nanoparticles
points: Size: 1-100 nm (nanometres) — similar size to large molecules
Very high surface area to volume ratio — more atoms on the surface → more reactive
Different properties to bulk material: different colour, lower melting point, stronger, better conductor
Examples: gold nanoparticles (red/purple, not gold colour), carbon nanotubes

sections.title: Uses and Risks
points: Uses: sunscreen (TiO₂ nanoparticles), medicines (drug delivery), catalysts, electronics, antibacterial surfaces
Risks: very small — might pass through cell membranes; long-term health effects unknown; environmental impact unclear
Ethical issue: benefits vs unknown risks — need more research

keyTerms.def: A particle 1-100 nm in size with a very high surface area to volume ratio
The ratio of surface area to volume — higher in smaller particles

examTips: Nanoparticles have high SA:V ratio — more reactive than bulk material.
Be able to evaluate nanoparticle use — benefits (sunscreen, medicines) vs risks (unknown long-term effects).
commonMistakes: Saying nanoparticles are the same as the bulk material — their properties are DIFFERENT.
